paras: The New York West Side race attacks of August 26, 1900 were assaults by groups of white men on Black residents around Amsterdam Avenue and West Sixtieth to Sixty-fourth streets in Manhattan, beginning before daybreak with the beating of James Arnold, a 55-year-old Black man. They followed the shooting of a white messenger boy, John Brennan, by a Black man known as "Lamplighter," and the Associated Press reported them nationally as "incipient race riots." Arnold and Alexander Balentine were badly beaten and a gang smashed the windows of a Black tenement, but no one was arrested for either beating.

Late on Saturday, August 25, a row broke out at Sixty-second Street and Amsterdam Avenue between Black men outside a clubhouse and young white men across the street. According to the Sun, a man said to be John Davis, known as "Lamplighter," fired five shots, one of which struck Brennan, 20, in the abdomen; the AP wrote that Brennan had been among whites who taunted Davis. In the wire's words, the shooting set "the rough white element" searching for Black people.

Early on Sunday, Arnold was passing Sixty-fourth Street and Amsterdam Avenue when a gang of white men attacked him. The Tribune reported that one shouted "Kill the black nigger!" and another declared Arnold the fugitive "Lamplighter," after which the gang beat him badly. A policeman drove the crowd off, but Arnold, "as much afraid of the policeman as of the mob," would not wait for an ambulance; he later had his wounds dressed at Roosevelt Hospital and went home. Shortly afterward, about two blocks away, Balentine, 32, was beaten and sent to the same hospital.

At 9:30 a.m. Frank McPyke, 21, led a gang to a five-story tenement occupied by Black families on West Sixtieth Street "with the avowed purpose of cleaning it out," smashing nearly all the windows and injuring one or two people before police arrested him. A second gang member, Henry Schubel, was arrested later, and the tenement's Black janitor, John H. Pierson, went into hiding after whites threatened him for complaining. In the afternoon Joseph Doyle, 18, stoned passers-by at Fifty-ninth Street and Eleventh Avenue, wounding two Black men before his arrest.

Separately, Policeman John J. Cleary arrested William Hopson, a Black man, for refusing to move on, and when residents of West Sixtieth Street tried to free him, Cleary used his club and drew his revolver. George Meyer, arrested as the leader of the rescue, reached the station with scalp wounds and a possible fractured skull, which Cleary said came from a fall.

The Sun reported that Magistrate Brann fined McPike $5 for throwing stones into houses where Black people lived. No arrest for the beatings of Arnold or Balentine, and no later report of Brennan's condition, appears in the coverage. Meanwhile, Police Board President York said the form of the investigation the Mayor had requested into the earlier August riots was undecided.

The AP account ran on August 27 in papers from New Haven and Worcester to Houston and Beatrice, Nebraska, and kept appearing in Raleigh, Shiner, Texas, and Danville, Pennsylvania, through August 30. Its headlines varied: the Houston Daily Post wrote "NEGROES ATTACKED IN DISCRIMINATION," an Evening Journal led with "CUCKOO ROW RESENTS ARREST," and the Montour American blamed "NEW YORK'S HOODLUMS."

In New York, the Tribune headlined "MORE ATTACKS ON NEGROES," printed the attackers' slurs and Cleary's explanation without comment, and quoted a Georgia minister saying the mob was "enough to shut the mouth of every South hater in the North." The Sun, by contrast, ran its story under "NEGROES SHOOT AND SLASH" and mentioned McPike only as a stone-throwing boy.

No Black paper in the coverage reported the August 26 attacks. Black weeklies treated the month's New York violence as police brutality, reprinting the Rev. W. Brooks's charge that "the clubbing in nearly every case was done by the police." The Cleveland Gazette quoted E. Lee saying few Black people had been hurt by white men compared with police clubs, and the Colored American and the Plaindealer blamed Tammany.
Some wire versions gave McPike's age as 24 rather than 21. Meyer's injuries are explained only by the arresting officer.

reader.title: New York West Side race attacks of August 26, 1900
bases: Gangs of white men beat Arnold and Balentine in the street, stoned Black passers-by and wrecked the windows of a Black tenement, injuring several people but killing no one (A1, A3).

The New-York Tribune's local account (A1) and the Associated Press wire (A3, A6) agree on the beatings of Arnold and Balentine and the tenement attack, and the Sun (A2) independently reports McPike's arrest for stoning houses occupied by Black residents.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune local report
accounts.gist: A gang attacked Arnold, one shouting 'Kill the black nigger!' and another calling him the fugitive 'Lamplighter'; it gives names, ages and addresses for victims and attackers and McPyke's boasts.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: The shooting of Brennan, one of a crowd of whites who had taunted Davis, set 'the rough white element' searching for Black people; Arnold and Ballentine were beaten and a tenement attacked.

accounts.label: The Sun
accounts.gist: Tells the Brennan shooting in detail and treats McPike only as a boy arrested for throwing stones into houses and fined $5; does not name Arnold or Balentine.

accounts.label: Policeman Cleary's account
accounts.gist: Cleary said Meyer led an attempted rescue, resisted, and 'fell down' on the way to the station, causing his head wounds.

accounts.label: Black press on the August riots
accounts.gist: Black papers did not name Arnold; they described the month's New York riots as attacks on Black residents compounded by police clubbing.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'MORE ATTACKS ON NEGROES' and 'AROUSES TOUGHS TO LAWLESSNESS', said the gang beat Arnold 'shamefully', and printed the attackers' slurs verbatim.

The AP wire called the clashes 'incipient race riots', traced them to the shooting, and described the victims as passing 'quietly'; local headlines ranged from 'NEGROES ATTACKED IN DISCRIMINATION' to 'CUCKOO ROW RESENTS ARREST' and 'NEW YORK'S HOODLUMS'.
The Sun led with 'NEGROES SHOOT AND SLASH', putting the Black shooter and a razor slashing at the center and leaving out the beatings of Arnold and Balentine.
Black papers blamed the police and Tammany for the August riots, reprinting Brooks's charges and the E. Lee delegation's protest, without reporting the August 26 attacks specifically.

record_check.dossier: Mob victims: Arnold, Balentine, Adam Johnson, two unnamed men wounded by Doyle, tenement residents. Hopson and Meyer were police arrestees, McPike was a perpetrator, and no Sarah Davis or Alex Valentine appears.

Arnold was attacked in the street while passing, not in custody

At least 4 by white attackers (Arnold, Balentine, two hit by Doyle), plus unnumbered heads cracked at the tenement; Meyer injured in police custody
Langtry struck by a brick in the evening; Brennan shot the night before

record_check.dossier: Those are the police reasons for arresting Hopson and Meyer; the attackers' stated reason for beating Arnold was that he was the fugitive 'Lamplighter'
